systems.name: The gaps between primes, as a return map
systems.summary: Each gap between consecutive primes plotted against the next, the way a chaotic flow's crossings are, beside a map that really has a rule. A cloud against a curve

blocks.label: The gaps
blocks.note: The primes found by a sieve, the gaps read off them. Every gap after the first is even

blocks.label: The return map
blocks.note: The same picture the Rossler page makes from a flow. A rule shows as a curve; the gaps show as a cloud on a grid of even numbers

blocks.label: How predictable the next gap is
blocks.note: The spread of the next gap once this one is known, over the spread with nothing known. A rule gives zero; the primes give a number close to one, the same as the shuffled gaps

blocks.label: How big the gaps run
blocks.note: The average gap near p is about the logarithm of p, the prime number theorem read as a spacing. The histogram's shape follows from that and little else

dimension.label: What chaos is not
dimension.note: A chaotic sequence has a rule and a positive exponent; two starts a hair apart follow the rule and part. The primes have no rule to follow, and the return map is how the two are told apart

definitions.name: The sieve
definitions.tex: \text{strike every multiple of each prime up to } \sqrt{N}
definitions.note: How the primes on the page are found: nothing is guessed, and nothing is looked up

definitions.name: A return map
definitions.note: Each value against the one that follows it. For a deterministic rule the points lie on the graph of that rule; this is the test the page applies
